question: What is the purpose of an  if  statement in Python?
correct: To run a block of code only when a condition is true
incorrect: To repeat a block of code until a condition is true
To give a name to a reusable block of code
To convert a value from one type into another
feedback: An if statement checks a condition and runs its indented block only when that condition evaluates to True.

question: In Python, the keyword used to provide an alternative condition after an  if  is:
incorrect: elseif
else if
elsef
feedback: Python uses elif (short for 'else if') to test another condition when the previous ones were false.

question: Trace this if/else. What does the program print?
feedback: x is 7, so the condition x > 10 is False and the else block runs, printing small.

question: Trace this if/elif/else chain. What does the program print?
feedback: score is 82: the first test (>= 90) fails, the elif (>= 80) succeeds, so B prints and the else is skipped.

question: Write the Python line that begins an if statement checking whether the variable x is greater than 0. (No body, just the header line.)
feedback: An if header is the keyword if, a condition, and a colon: if x > 0:

question: What is a nested decision?
correct: An if statement placed inside another if statement
incorrect: A loop that runs a second loop inside its body
A function that calls a second function by name
A condition combining two tests with the word and
feedback: Nesting means putting one decision inside another, so the inner condition is only checked when the outer one is true.

question: What is the value of  (5 > 3) and (2 > 4)  in Python?
incorrect: True
feedback: and is True only when both sides are True. The first part is True but the second (2 > 4) is False, so the whole expression is False.

question: What is the value of  not (3 == 3)  in Python?
incorrect: True
None
feedback: 3 == 3 is True, and not flips it to False.

question: Which of the following expressions evaluate to True? (Select all that apply)
feedback: or needs just one true side, not flips its value, and and needs both sides true. The two wrong options fail because the 'and' has a false side and 6 > 4 is true (so 'not' makes it false).

question: A program guards a division by writing  if count > 0 and total / count > 5:. Why does this avoid a divide-by-zero error?
correct: and stops as soon as a test is False, so the division never runs when count is 0
incorrect: and always evaluates both tests, but ignores any error the second one raises
Swapping the two tests would change nothing, because and ignores the order given
The division happens first, since arithmetic is evaluated before any comparison
feedback: Short-circuiting is what makes the guard work, and it is why the order of the two tests is not interchangeable here: the cheap safety check has to come first.

question: Python uses short-circuit evaluation. In  A or B, when is B skipped?
correct: When A is already True, since the result is True anyway
incorrect: When A is False, since B can no longer change it
When A and B are both numbers instead of conditions
When B appears earlier in the program than A does
feedback: For 'or', if A is True the whole expression is True, so Python does not bother evaluating B. (For 'and', it short-circuits when A is False.)

question: Match each boolean operator to how it decides its result.

pairs.definition: True only when both sides are true
True when at least one side is true
Reverses the truth value it is given

feedback: These three operators combine and flip conditions to build more complex tests.

question: What is the main difference between a  for  loop and a  while  loop?
correct: A for loop runs over a sequence; a while loop on a condition
incorrect: A for loop counts upward; a while loop counts downward
A while loop tests its condition once, before the first pass
A for loop must be given a range; it cannot walk a list
feedback: Use a for loop when you know what to iterate over (like a range), and a while loop when you repeat until some condition changes.
The inner loop runs all 4 of its passes for each of the outer loop's 3 passes, so the print runs 3 x 4 = 12 times. Nested loops multiply; they do not add.

question: What does  range(2, 6)  produce in Python?
incorrect: The numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
The numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
The numbers 2 and 6 only
feedback: range(a, b) starts at a and stops just before b, so range(2, 6) gives 2, 3, 4, 5.

question: The keyword that immediately exits a loop entirely is ___.
feedback: break stops the loop right away and continues with the code after the loop.

question: The keyword that skips the rest of the current loop pass and starts the next one is ___.
feedback: continue jumps back to the top of the loop for the next iteration without finishing the current one.

question: This loop skips some values with continue. What does the program print?
feedback: continue jumps straight to the next item, so the two negative values never reach the addition line. Only 3 and 4 are accumulated.

question: This loop breaks early. What does the program print?
feedback: It prints 0, 1 and 2 on separate lines, then i becomes 3, break fires, and the loop exits before 3 is ever printed.

question: Which of the following would cause an infinite loop? (Select all that apply)
correct: A while True loop with no break inside it
A while loop whose condition variable never changes
incorrect: A for loop running over range(10)
A while loop that decreases a counter toward zero
An if statement whose condition is false
feedback: An infinite loop never stops: while True with no break, or a while whose condition never becomes false. A for loop over a range ends naturally, and an if is not a loop.

question: A loop walks a list of readings and should ignore any negative reading while still processing everything after it. Which statement belongs inside the if?
correct: continue, which abandons this pass and moves on to the next item
incorrect: break, which leaves the loop at once so later items go unseen
return, which ends this pass and resumes with the next item
pass, which skips the rest of the pass just as continue does
feedback: The task is to skip one item, not to stop early, so the loop must keep going. pass is a do-nothing placeholder and changes no control flow at all.

question: NPC: Counting the passes of a loop
intro: Ada crouches over a corridor of numbered flagstones. “Loops are where apprentices lose their footing. Not because loops are hard — because they guess instead of counting. Count with me.”

steps.say:
Here is the loop:
for i in range(5):
    print(i)
range(5) hands out 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops BEFORE 5. Five values, so five passes.

beats.say: range(5) hands out 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 0 and stops BEFORE 5. Five values, so five passes.

steps.say: Now a two-part range: range(2, 6). It starts at 2 and still stops before the second number: 2, 3, 4, 5.

check.prompt: So how many passes does for i in range(2, 6) make?
check.why: Subtract the start from the stop: 6 - 2 = 4. The stop value is a door you halt at, never step through.

steps.say: That gives you the whole rule. For range(stop), the count is the stop value. For range(start, stop), the count is stop - start. Count the values first, then worry about what the body does with them.

beats.say: That gives you the whole rule. For range(stop), the count is the stop value. For range(start, stop), the count is stop - start.
Count the values first, then worry about what the body does with them.

outro: “The monsters ahead deal in loop counts. Don't guess — subtract.”

feedback_template: range(a, b) goes from {{a}} up to but not including {{b}}, giving {{b}} minus {{a}} = {{expected}} values.

A loop runs  for i in range({{start}}, {{stop}}, {{step}}). How many times does its body run?
feedback_template: Stepping by {{step}} from {{start}} up to (not including) {{stop}} gives {{expected}} iterations.

feedback_template: Each pass removes {{step}} from n, and {{start}} divided by {{step}} is {{expected}}, so the body runs {{expected}} times before n reaches 0 and the test fails.

question: Write the Python line that begins an endless loop using the while keyword and the value True. (Just the header line.)
feedback: while True: loops forever unless a break inside the body stops it.

question: What is the main purpose of a function?
correct: To bundle reusable steps under a name you can call
incorrect: To repeat a block of code a fixed number of times
To store a single value for use later in the program
To convert one Python data type into another type
feedback: A function packages a task under a name. Once defined, you can call it as many times as you need instead of repeating the code.

question: Write the Python header line that defines a function named f that takes no parameters. (Just the def line, no body.)
feedback: A function definition uses def, the name, parentheses for parameters, and a colon: def f():

question: Write the Python header line that defines a function named f with one parameter n whose default value is 1. (Just the def line, no body.)
feedback: The default is written as an assignment inside the parentheses, and the header still ends with a colon before the indented body.

question: In the definition  def greet(name):, what is  name?
correct: A parameter that receives a value when greet is called
incorrect: The value that the function sends back to the caller
A global variable that the whole program shares
The name of the function that is being defined
feedback: name is a parameter: a placeholder that receives the argument passed in when greet is called.

question: What does the  return  statement do in a function?
correct: It sends a value back to the caller and ends the function
incorrect: It prints a value to the screen for the user to read
It runs the function again from its very first line
It stores a value in a permanent global variable
feedback: return hands a value back to the caller and immediately exits the function. Returning is not the same as printing.

question: A function ends with  print(total)  where it should have said  return total. The caller then runs  x = compute(4). What is x?
correct: None, because a function that returns no value hands back None
incorrect: The printed number, since print sends the value back to the caller
0, because Python gives a missing return value the value zero
An error, because assigning from a function requires a return
feedback: print sends characters to the screen; return sends a value to whoever called the function. The two are easy to confuse because both seem to 'produce' the number.

question: Write the Python statement that returns the value of the variable x from a function.
feedback: return x sends the value of x back to whatever called the function.

question: A function is defined as  def total(a, b={{d}}):  with the single body line  return a * b. What value does the call  total({{a}})  return?
feedback_template: Only one argument is supplied, so b falls back to its default of {{d}}, and the function returns {{a}} * {{d}} = {{expected}}.

question: NPC: What really happens when you call a function
intro: Ada pulls a lever and a hatch opens in the floor. “A function call looks like one line. It is actually five separate things happening in order, and if you can name them, no call can surprise you.”

steps.say:
Take this pair:
def triple(n):
    return n * 3

print(triple(4))
When Python reaches triple(4), it first works out the argument — the value 4 — before anything else happens.

beats.say: When Python reaches triple(4), it first works out the argument — the value 4 — before anything else happens.

steps.say: Then it binds that value to the parameter name: inside the function, n IS 4. The body runs with that binding and reaches return n * 3, which computes 12.

check.prompt: The body has computed 12 and hit return. What happens next?
check.answer: The value 12 is sent back and print() receives it
wrong: The function keeps running its remaining lines
The value 12 is stored in the variable n
check.why: return does two things at once: it hands the value back to the caller and ends the function immediately.

steps.say: Then the paused line resumes with the returned value in hand, and print shows 12. Argument, bind, run, return, resume — five beats, always the same five.

outro: “Trace those five beats and the next question is bookkeeping, not guesswork.”

question: Arrange what Python does, in order, when a call like triple(4) runs.
items: Evaluate the argument to get a value
Bind that value to the parameter name
Run the statements in the function body
Send the returned value back to the caller
Resume the line that made the call
feedback: A call is five beats in a fixed order: work out the argument, bind it to the parameter, run the body, return a value, and resume the paused caller with that value in hand.

question: Arrange these lines into a working program that defines a function and prints its result.
feedback: The header comes first, then the indented body: check the condition, return a when it holds, otherwise fall through to return b. The call can only run after the definition exists.

question: This program calls a function. What does it print?
feedback: double(6) computes 6 * 2 and returns 12, which print then displays.

question: In  def power(base, exp=2):, what does the  exp=2  part mean?
correct: exp gets a default of 2 when the caller supplies nothing
incorrect: exp must be exactly 2 and cannot be changed by a caller
exp is compared to 2 each time the function runs
the function returns 2 whenever exp is left out
feedback: A default value lets a parameter be optional: if the caller omits exp, it is 2; if they pass a value, that value is used instead.

question: Which of the following are true about Python functions? (Select all that apply)
correct: A function can take zero or more parameters
A function can return a value with return
A function can be called many times after being defined once
incorrect: A function must always include a return statement
A function can be defined only once per program run
feedback: Functions may take any number of parameters, may or may not return a value, and are reusable. A function without a return statement still runs; it just hands back None.

question: What is a docstring?
correct: A string at the top of a function saying what it does
incorrect: A string that Python prints each time the function is called
A comment marked with # placed just above the def line
A string handed back to the caller when there is no return
feedback: A docstring is a string written as the first line of a function body to describe its purpose for anyone reading the code.

question: What does it mean to call a function using a keyword argument, as in  power(base=3, exp=4)?
correct: Each argument is matched by name rather than by position
incorrect: Each argument name must be a reserved Python keyword
The parameters base and exp are given new default values
The values are still matched by position, and the names ignored
feedback: Keyword arguments name the parameter they fill (base=3, exp=4), so order does not matter and the call is easier to read.

question: A value written inside the parentheses of a function call, which is handed to the matching parameter, is called an ___.
feedback: Parameters are the names in the def line; arguments are the actual values supplied at the moment of the call. One name, many different arguments over a program's life.

question: A function reassigns its parameter. What does the program print?
code:
def change(n):
    n = n + 1

x = 5
change(x)
print(x)
feedback: Inside change, n is a local variable; reassigning it does not affect x outside. So x is still 5 when printed. This is variable scope.

question: Why can't code outside a function use a variable that was created inside that function?
correct: Variables made inside a function are local and exist only while it runs
incorrect: The variable is global, but only the function may print its value
Outside code must call the function again before reading the value
The name does exist outside, but it still holds its pre-call value
feedback: A variable created inside a function has local scope: it exists only during that call, so outside code cannot see it.

question: A variable created inside a function, invisible to code outside it, is called a ___ variable.
feedback: A local variable lives only for the duration of the call that created it. That is why code outside the function cannot see it, and why two calls never share one.

question: In  def scale(v, factor=3):, the 3 makes factor a {{1}} value, used whenever the caller supplies only v; meanwhile a variable first assigned inside scale is {{2}}, so it disappears once the call ends.
feedback: These are two separate ideas that both live in the def line's neighbourhood: defaults decide what happens when an argument is missing, while scope decides how long a name inside the body survives.

question: Which three building blocks are enough, on their own, to express any algorithm?
incorrect: Variables, comments, and print statements
Integers, strings, and booleans
Input, output, and storage
feedback: Running steps in order (sequence), choosing a branch (selection), and repeating (iteration) are a complete set — a result proved in 1966. No fourth kind of control flow is needed, which is why jumping around with goto fell out of use.

question: The same five lines that convert a temperature appear in four places in a program. Why is moving them into one function the better design?
correct: The rule is written once, so a fix or a change happens in exactly one place
incorrect: Calling one function four times runs faster than four copies of the lines
With one function the conversion runs once instead of running four times
A fix applied to one of the four copies spreads to the other three
feedback: This is the DRY principle — Don't Repeat Yourself. With four copies you have four chances to fix a bug in three of them; with one function there is a single place to get right, and a single place to test.

question: Why should you test a function against edge cases (like 0, an empty input, or a very large value)?
correct: Ordinary inputs may work while unusual ones reveal hidden bugs
incorrect: Empty and zero inputs are the only values Python checks at runtime
A passing test on 0 also covers every negative number below it
An empty input makes Python skip the function body automatically
feedback: Code that handles typical inputs can still fail on boundaries like empty or zero values, so testing edge cases catches bugs before they ship.
